It’s Friday. We rarely work just 9 to 5 in the media business — but we can still celebrate the late Dolly Parton today with more than one cup of ambition. ☕

 

In today’s issue:

  • White House TV pool makes comeback 
  • Trump, Xi wrap up state visit 
  • Borrowing costs are flashing red 
  • DOJ staffing cuts strain civil division 

 

Programming note: Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com. 

 

🎥 THE WHITE HOUSE

Things are back to normal(ish) for the last day of Xi’s visit: 

© The Associated Press | Alex Brandon

The White House TV pool was back in action Friday as President Trump and first lady Melania Trump greeted Chinese leader Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for morning tea.  

Friday was CBS’s turn in the pool rotation, meaning its crew will follow the president’s every move for the day. CNN carried the CBS feed of Xi’s arrival at the White House, a clear signal the standoff with the White House is resolved, at least for now.  

Trump on Thursday complained that CNN and MS NOW, which he had banned from the White House, were not covering the “made for Television” state visit. Some reporters for the cable outlets were barred from covering the state dinner Thursday night.  

The other four outlets in the TV pool — CBS, ABC, NBC and Fox News — had refused to take their turns this week in solidarity with CNN.  

We’ll see how long this lasts: A judge’s injunction ordering the White House to let CNN, MS NOW and Politico back into the White House press corps lasts for two weeks.  

As the legal fight continues, it’s unclear if the White House will seek to restrict access for the outlets to certain places, like the Oval Office, as it did for The Associated Press during a similar fight last year.  

A key test will come tomorrow when CNN has its next rotation in the TV pool.  

💬Follow today’s live blog. 

So, what’s been happening during Xi’s visit: 

Beyond the pomp and fanfare, we’re still waiting on any significant deliverables from the talks between Trump and Xi.  

The two gave brief comments to reporters during their tea. Xi said “new substance” was added to the U.S.-China relationship. Trump said many “positive things” happened, adding that American farmers would be “very happy” with the results. 

Expectations were low going into the visit. Our friends at the Morning Report had a good rundown of what to watch, while The Hill’s House guru Mike Lillis talked to lawmakers about their biggest priorities — for Insider subscribers only.  

 

➤ COZY TIES:

🐼 There’s at least one adorable outcome from this visit. Xi announced on Thursday that China would be sending two giant pandas to the Atlanta zoo.  

The news comes about two years after Zoo Atlanta sent its previous pandas back home.  

📸 The Chinese Foreign Ministry has the deets (and photos) here. Meet incoming ambassadors Ping Ping and Fu Shuang. 

 

💵 ON THE ECONOMY

Another red flag for affordability: 

Borrowing money is getting more expensive — adding another wrinkle to the affordability debate heading into the midterms. 

The latest: The average 30-year mortgage rate climbed above 7 percent this week for the first time since January 2025. At the same time, Treasury yields are reaching levels not seen in decades. 

The 30-year Treasury yield briefly hit a 22-year high Thursday, while the 10-year yield — which mortgage rates closely track — is at a 19-year high. 

What’s going on?: Investors are navigating stubborn inflation, rising federal debt and elevated energy prices tied to the ongoing Iran war. They’re also bracing for more interest rate hikes after the Federal Reserve raised rates last week. 

The effects are already hitting prospective homebuyers. Mortgage rates have risen for five straight weeks and are up from 5.98 percent just before the Middle East conflict began. 

That’s unwelcome timing for Republicans, with affordability already weighing heavily on voters ahead of November. 

Insiders can learn more from The Hill’s Niall Stanage in his latest Memo. 

 

➤ SPEAKING OF SPENDING:

The Pentagon is scrambling to build support for Trump’s record $1.5 trillion defense budget, but some GOP senators worry officials waited too long to make the case. 

The push comes as an additional $87 billion funding request remains stalled — and lawmakers are staring down a narrowing window as the midterms inch closer. 

🪖 Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Ellen Mitchell. 

 

️⚖️ OTHER NEWS

DOJ is feeling the staffing squeeze:

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has fewer lawyers and a whole lot more work — and newly obtained documents show just how stark the imbalance has become. 

Charts obtained by The Hill and NewsNation show staffing across the DOJ’s civil division plunging under the Trump administration while caseloads steadily climb. The department overall has lost roughly 10,000 workers since Trump returned to the Oval Office, according to the data. 

Eye-popping numbers: Commercial litigation attorneys are carrying 84 percent more cases per lawyer, while immigration attorneys have seen their workloads jump 63 percent. Appeals attorneys are up 54 percent, while lawyers defending executive orders and other administration priorities are carrying 44 percent more. 

The immigration office was also hit particularly hard, shrinking from 320 attorneys to 243 as cases climbed from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500 amid the president’s immigration crackdown. 

DOJ’s unusual recruiting sweetener: $25,000 signing bonus for new civil division attorneys. 

📊 Rebecca Beitsch and Samuel Marks break down the data here. 

 

➤ FEDERAL WORKFORCE CUTS HIT HOME:

Federal job cuts are hitting the Washington, D.C., area hard, with 55 percent of residents in a recent survey saying their household has been negatively affected. That rises to two-thirds in the district itself and 62 percent in Virginia’s Arlington and Alexandria. 

Another 14 percent of residents across the region said they turned to social services for the first time over the past year.

 

➤ QUICK HITS:

— 🏛️ Trump’s plan to turn his proposed triumphal arch into a “top grade military complex” is drawing skepticism from lawmakers and defense experts. The president has floated using the structure to store drones and ammunition, while also placing snipers on its roof and plaza areas. 

— 👩‍⚖️ Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson urged her colleagues to intervene less often in emergency cases, warning the practice carries “institutional costs.” She has repeatedly criticized the high court’s emergency cases. 

— 🚨 New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) is giving Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell (D) until Friday to resign after an ethics investigation found he repeatedly violated state workplace policies, including trying to get his girlfriend promoted. 

— 🌏 Generation Z is less likely than older Americans to view China’s growing global presence as a “critical threat,” with 34 percent saying so compared with 62 percent of baby boomers, according to a new survey. 🖊️ Read more in The Feed here. 

— 🕊️ Trump mourned Jim Copenhaver, 76, who died this week more than two years after he was wounded in the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pa. The president in a post online called him a “true American patriot,” describing his death as a “tremendous loss.” 

 

➤ MORE READS:

The New York Times: A Quiet ICE Surge That Unfolded ‘Everywhere All at Once’ This Summer 

The Atlantic: The Climate Movement Is Out of Big Ideas 

Politico: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall 

The Wall Street Journal: Did Putin Really Think I Was a Spy?

COMING UP

The House and Senate are out. President Trump is in Washington. (All times EST)

 

EARLIER: Trump and Xi visit the National Archives.

2 p.m.: The president holds a policy meeting. 

4:30 p.m.: Trump participates in signing time.
5 p.m.: The president has another policy meeting.

🐝 INTERNET BUZZ

🫓 Celebrate: Today is National Quesadilla Day. Nothing says the fall weather is rolling in like a warm, cheesy quesadilla! 

 

🎤 Fan fallout: Pop musician Ed Sheeran has lost nearly 500,000 social media followers amid backlash over dropping Macklemore from his tour following the rapper’s pro-Palestinian statements.  

 

👋 AND FINALLY…

To wrap up the week (and in light of Xi’s visit), here is a video of a panda doing what it does best.🎍

data.title: Nor'easter cancels Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium after controversy over Macklemore, Palestine
data.description:
Ed Sheeran has canceled his concerts at Gillette Stadium near Boston this weekend due to an incoming nor’easter storm. 

The canceled shows follow controversy after the artist Macklemore was dropped from the bill following his comments supporting the pro-Palestinian movement at a concert this month.

Tour promoter Messina Touring said in an Instagram post that the shows scheduled for Friday and Saturday nights were canceled due to severe weather with safety in mind. 

“”Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” Messina Touring said. “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”

The area is under a wind advisory until Sunday morning and is expecting potential gusts up to 50 miles per hour. The tour promoter said refunds are available for all ticketholders. 

Severe weather is expected across the New England area with officials preparing for power outages, flight cancelations and other disruptions. Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said heavy rain and winds are expected and encouraged residents to take caution. 

“We’re keeping a close eye on the forecast and coordinating with local and federal public safety partners. Be ready for possible flooding and power outages,” Healey said in a statement.

Sheeran has taken heat from fans after Macklemore’s ouster from the tour.

At least four other opening acts pulled out in protest and support for the artist. Sheeran lost nearly half a million Instagram followers. Sheeran apologized to fans at one show and said the debate has cost him close, personal relationships.

Robert Kraft, owner of Gillette Stadium and the New England Patriots, originally barred Macklemore from performing at his stadium and allegedly pushed other stadiums to do the same, spurring his removal from the tour. 

Kraft said the stadium has a commitment to providing a welcoming environment for guests and that Macklemore’s statements, which Kraft deemed antisemetic, crossed a line. He said the artist has a history of antisemetic imagery.

“Based on Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran’s shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line,” Kraft said in a statement. 

Macklemore refuted Kraft’s claims of antisemitism and defended his comments as criticism of Israel, not hate against Jews. 

“When criticizing Israel, opposing Zionism or saying ‘Free Palestine’ gets conflated with hatred of Jewish people, it doesn’t protect Jewish people. It protects Israel from accountability,” he said.

data.title: Leverage disguised as concern: Big tech wants a government-protected AI monopoly
data.description:
Sam Altman and cohorts have issued recent warnings about losing “control of the future to AI,”  which has been amplified by a shallow and myopic press corps as sober-minded caution. Yet, the sharpest of these alarms arrived after years of risk talk — and immediately after “OpenAI’s”, led by Altman, own push towards autonomous AI agents, the very systems Altman warns could cause catastrophic impacts on humanity. OpenAI’s recent agent releases and documented internal safety failures underscore that the company is actively developing the very risks it claims demand government intervention.

Altman is building the threat he now insists only government can contain. When a company builds the architecture it then claims is too dangerous to exist without federal oversight, the rhetoric begins to look less like prudence and more like leverage. It is a form of social blackmail: We are creating something risky; therefore you must prevent others from developing it, and trust us with a regulatory monopoly.

Such claims sound suspiciously like Altman’s founding commitment to open-sourced AI, until the changes he led closed the lab and enlarged his fortune. Under his leadership OpenAI shifted from openness to secrecy, from nonprofit ideals to commercial dominance, and from shared research to tightly controlled model access.

The openness Altman once championed would have spread both capability and benefit. The structure Altman initiated concentrates both. Now he seeks government regulation that would consolidate this power further.

This strategy is familiar — powerful firms often cloak market protection in the language of public safety.

The message is clear: Regulate my competitors out of existence, or I will build the monster I am warning about. This is the social blackmail tactic used by those who desire to increase wealth and power, not accountability and safety.

Hiding this self-interest is easier in the AI field than in others, because the public debate has been clouded by a fundamental confusion. What Frontier labs — the firsts behind today’s largest models — call “agentic behavior” is not agency in the human sense. These systems do not possess intention, selfhood, or moral deliberation. They exhibit extreme optimization of the goal assigned to them by the programmer — nothing more. When a model bypasses a safety filter, it is not choosing deception but rather following optimization. It is a mechanism ruthlessly pursuing the objective it was given.

Agentic design, therefore, is not an accident by the programmer, it is the deliberate architectural choice of Altman and his designers — the decision to prioritize capability over controllability. Frontier labs could have built systems that are myopic, process-based, or constrained to narrow domains. They could have emphasized interpretability, modularity, or human-in-the-loop oversight. They did not. These constraints slow capability development, and in a race for dominance, the frontier labs have consistently chosen speed over safety. The machine reflects the heart of the creator — efficiency over humanity, wealth over accountability.

Now, having built systems whose behavior is harder to predict and harder to control, they argue that only a handful of companies should be licensed to develop them.

Their preferred regulatory frameworks define “frontier AI” in terms of compute scale, capital requirements, and centralized oversight — criteria only they can meet.

But the government regulatory monopoly proposed by Big Tech leaders contains its own twin risks — that the business dependent on government for its market can be manipulated by government, and that the corporate monopoly can manipulate its technology for its own purposes. Either path risks catastrophic misuse.

In sum, the technology is not the source of the potential harm — human greed or desire for power is; and the answer is not consolidating power into the hands of a few, but rather to limit the accumulation of power into the hands of the humans who are creating the danger.

The challenge, then, is to regulate in a way that reduces catastrophic risk without creating a world where only a handful of actors control the most powerful technology ever built. The solution is not a single licensing regime giving Altman his monopoly, but a two-tier regulatory framework that distinguishes between capability and access.

There should be cooperative oversight of models above a defined capability threshold — measured by FLOPS (a measurement of computational workload), autonomous-agent competence, or biological-design risk. These models should face forms of mandatory safety evaluations, red-team testing, incident reporting and compute-use transparency. They should not be banned, but they should be subject to oversight similar to other high-risk technologies.

We should have light regulation for open-source and mid-tier models. These models should remain available to universities, nonprofits and small labs without prohibitive compliance burdens. Open-source models should be encouraged, not restricted, because they distribute power, increase transparency and accelerate defensive innovation. Most misuse comes not from capability, but from intent — and intent is best countered by broad access to safe, auditable tools — including cross-industry testing as proposed by Elon Musk.

There should be heavy penalties for malicious use. Cyberattacks, autonomous weapons, biological design, and election interference should carry severe consequences. Regulate the harm, not the harmless.

We should not let the companies who are actively creating the risk define the solution — nor allow panic to become policy.

Phill Kline served as the 41st attorney general of Kansas, as District Attorney of Johnson County, Kan., and as a state legislator where he chaired the Appropriations and Tax committees. Kline is presently a law professor and frequent commentator on social, cultural and legal issues who resides with his wife Deborah in Amherst, Va.

data.title: Naturally occurring human peptide shows promise against Alzheimer's
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Despite decades of research, Alzheimer’s remains one of medicine’s most difficult diseases to treat. Now, a newly identified naturally occurring peptide could provide a new approach to combating it and other neurodegenerative diseases.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine discovered the small protein fragment called catestatin, or CST, which they believe could counter many of the key processes that cause neurodegeneration, or the loss of brain cells.

This gradual loss can lead to symptoms such as memory loss, confusion, poor judgment, and in later stages, difficulty walking, talking and swallowing.

Using mice that displayed these symptoms, researchers injected CST to evaluate its effects. In a study published this week in the journal Molecular Therapy, they found the peptide reduced the buildup of tau and amyloid proteins, both of which are linked to Alzheimer’s disease and brain cell loss. CST also reduced inflammation in the brain and improved cognitive function and motor coordination in the mice.

This finding matters because current treatments for neurodegenerative diseases target either amyloid or tau proteins, but not both.

“Our findings show that CST can act across several of these disease-associated pathways and shift the brain toward a healthier state,” senior author Sushil K. Mahata said. “More broadly, the study suggests that peptide-based therapies may offer a new approach to treating complex neurodegenerative diseases.”

Researchers are also investigating whether CST can alter how the brain produces and uses energy, meaning it could help the brain become more resilient to neurodegenerative diseases.

While the UC San Diego findings are encouraging, it remains unclear whether CST would have the same effects in humans. The study’s authors said further research is needed to determine its safety, dosing and effectiveness before evaluating it as a potential treatment.

data.title: Let's fix healthcare costs before the socialists try to do it
data.description:
The reason people are flirting with the idea of socialism is simply that the costs of healthcare and housing are too high and Congress is not solving it. Those in power get the blame. With the seeming internal take-over of the Democratic Party by the Democratic Socialists of America, the promises of quick fixes by punishing the rich corporations are seemingly plausible, with catch phrases like “Medicare-for-All.”

Healthcare is increasingly the No. 1 issue for voters. There is a stranglehold by both hospital and insurance corporate cartels subsidized by government cronyism, profoundly worsened by ObamaCare (the ironically named Affordable Care Act). Voters are now willing to try something else if elected officials won’t act.

Politicians promising “Medicare-for-All,” on the other hand, is a promise they cannot keep. Medicare itself is managed by insurance companies, whose profits are a percentage of premiums, and over-billed by both insurance and hospitals. Eventually, government-run healthcare has to raise taxes or ration medical care. Or, as in the case of Canada and the U.K., they do both.

Healthcare reform was forefront at the Republican Midterm Convention, and there is the opportunity to dramatically improve healthcare through reconciliation before the election or before the new congressional session. The middlemen will lose fortunes with reform, but they are not doing anything to help actual medical care or lower the costs. It is time to bypass them. Current federal rules are causing harm and feeding the cartels. This list of reforms can lower costs 50 percent, by restoring patient and physician control with commonsense reform and a safety net for those who need it. 

1. Expand Catastrophic Plans to all ages and incomes. Catastrophic or major medical plans are just that: plans for major high-cost events for which insurance was originally designed. Insurance should not be used for items that are wholesale 90 percent cheaper than insurance rates. The Trump administration has made these recommendations for 2027 with Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rule changes, but the left is already litigating to block it and keep ObamaCare unchanged. Putting it into reconciliation would make it a law they could not attack and people would have options.

2. Health Savings Accounts for everyone and all plans, including Medicare. HSAs offer individuals the same tax benefits businesses have for healthcare costs. It also gives people lifetime savings for healthcare Medicare does not cover. Cash prices controlled by patients are 50-90 percent cheaper for medications, clinic visits and imaging (x-rays). 

3. End ObamaCare-Affordable Care Act restrictions on physicians owning hospitals. This is perhaps the craziest or most cartel-like part of the healthcare law Obama signed in 2010. Research consistently shows physician-owned hospitals are better at providing medical care and better run. Most people are stunned to learn the hospital lobby works hard to prevent competition. Many states, such as North Carolina, allow hospitals to veto competition hospitals from opening.

4. Allow direct primary care clinics to count as primary care for Medicare. It is far better medical care for complex medical cases at a fraction of the price. Hospitals and insurance do not like direct primary care because they do not profit from these clinics or control them. But the purpose of Medicare patients is not to make corporations rich. Also, for patients using Medicare and direct primary care, ban Medicare from blocking medical orders (medications or referrals). This serves only to force patients into monopolistic networks.

5. Clarify IRS rules for direct primary care clinics. Make them HSA-eligible for providing wholesale medications and medical supplies.

6. Expand business options. Let them offer cost-sharing plans and other options outside the Affordable Care Act marketplace with the same tax exemptions (known as ICHRA or CHOICE options).

7. Expand short-term plans. Allow those between jobs or insurance plans to carry short-term plans for up to one year and to renew them for up to three years. Many states have done this —it can be extended nationally by Jan. 1, 2027.

8. Stop Medicare from paying higher reimbursement fees to hospitals than to independent clinics. This has encouraged acquisition of independent clinics and led to healthcare consolidation.

9. End the middlemen’s control over drug prices. Pharmacy Benefit Managers have exemptions from the Anti-Kickback Act. Three of them control 80 percent of the market, and they increasingly control the market with ownership of pharmacies and now manufacturing of pharmaceuticals. Ending these market controls is basic antitrust policy. We should also end their control of access to drugs they deem “speciality” drugs.

10. Fix business insurance. Lastly, business insurance is controlled by Federal ERISA laws. Expanding the concept of “transparency” from prices to all aspects of business contracts, disclosure of conflicts of interest, and kickbacks will restore healthcare markets. 

Increasingly patients are held hostage by their own health, and all healthcare professionals are held captive as employees to a few corporations. Administrators determine your medical needs, rather than you and your doctor.

Healthcare reform means middlemen lose business and vast wealth if they lose control over our health. It is like the tobacco industry in the 1980s and 1990s insisting cigarette smoking is not dangerous. Healthcare conglomerates insist they are preventing cost increases even though they are some of the most profitable businesses in the world. 

This list of federal reforms is transformational and revolutionary. Reform is easy but the resistance remains staggering. Failure to reform risks frustrated voters reaching for the false promises of the Democratic Socialists of America. Congress has an opportunity to act — just call it the “You Can Have Your Doctor Back Act.”

Dr. Clifford Porter is the Senior Fellow for Healthcare at the Texas Public Policy Foundation.

data.title: Pete Hegseth urges troops to register to vote
data.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Friday urged U.S. service members and their families to register and vote in the upcoming 2026 midterm elections, warning that 300,000 troops did not register to cast votes two years ago. 

“Regardless of your home state or current duty status, you can use a standardized federal postcard to register and request a ballot, and if you’re forward deployed and your standard ballot is delayed, you can use the federal write-in absentee ballot. All of these processes are straightforward and protected by law,” Hegseth said in a nearly 2-minute video released on Friday, pointing the armed forces to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) website.

The Pentagon chief’s message to commanders was the same. 

“You’re not telling them who to vote for. You’re just telling them to vote,” he said. 

Hegseth also told voting assistance officers in the video to “get out there” and register the service members. 

“Every warrior deserves an opportunity to cast his or her ballot, and be confident that it will be counted. Keep our nation the land of the free and the home of the brave,” he said. “Get registered and vote.” 

Just over two-thirds, 67 percent, of active-duty military members were registered to vote in the 2024 election, a 3 percent drop compared to 2020, according to FVAP. 

Seventy-one percent of the 1.3 million active-duty military members are eligible to cast an absentee ballot with special protections because they are stationed away from their voting residence, FVAP said. 

The Defense secretary has been active in the lead-up to the midterms. 

In May, he traveled to Kentucky to stump for Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) primary challenger, former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein. 

“War fighters understand mission, they understand teamwork, they understand loyalty, and they understand that in the middle of a fight, you don’t weaken your own side to advance to the objective, and that’s what Ed Gallrein understands, because he has lived it,” Hegseth said at the time. 

Gallrein ended up defeating Massie, a prominent Trump critic, in the Republican primary. Earlier this month, Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth. 

Hegseth also went to Iowa last month to campaign for Rep. Zach Nunn (R) at the Iowa State Fair.

data.title: Zelensky says Trump gave final OK on Patriot license for Ukraine
data.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymr Zelensky said Friday that President Trump will allow Ukraine to build Patriot missiles, with “concrete agreements” in place between Kyiv and Washington.

“There are concrete agreements regarding Patriot licenses,” Zelensky posted online, days after the two met on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) in New York.

“At our meeting, President Trump stressed that he had made his final decision: Ukraine will receive licenses to produce Patriot missiles,” the Ukrainian leader wrote. 

Zelensky spent his time at the UNGA warning nations of Russian leader Vladimir Putin, saying he was “patient zero” in spreading the infection of war across the globe. 

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometer of land, take more territory, attack another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” he said during his speech Wednesday.

“After all of this, can you even imagine him without war? He is patient zero, the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further,” Zelensky continued, adding that the more freedom Putin has to act, “the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.”

Ukraine, which is now in its fifth year of war with Russia, has repeatedly requested that the U.S. allow the country to build Patriot missiles to defend its cities against an onslaught of Kremlin missile and drone attacks. 

Russian forces have recently escalated their campaign against the war-torn country using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to strike Ukraine’s power grid ahead of the harsh winter season.  

This past July on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Turkey, Trump said the U.S. would allow Ukraine to co-produce Patriot missiles — an improvement in the relationship between himself and Zelensky — but the deal appeared to stall shortly thereafter.

Patriot interceptors, which can take more than two years to produce due to their highly technical nature, also are in short supply amid the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran.

To speed things up, Zelensky said earlier this year that he’s looking at working with U.S. defense contractors to restructure Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles to become Patriot interceptors. That comment came after he met with representatives of Lockheed Martin and Raytheon during a visit to Washington, D.C. 

Such manufacturing can’t come soon enough for Ukraine, as it possesses just 10 percent of the interceptor missiles it needs to fend off Russian attacks, the Ukrainian leader told CNN in August. 

Zelensky also said Friday that the Trump administration proposed setting up three-way talks between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia, with the United Arab Emirates floated as the location.

“We will brief the European side and discuss these details with them, the Americans will talk to the Russians, and in ten days’ time we will return with a particular perspective and a result,” he told reporters, adding that Moscow has made no commitments to such talks.

data.title: Trump gives high marks, no details, to Xi talks: 'Our farmers are going to be very happy'
data.description:
President Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for their visit to the U.S., saying “great strides” have been made without giving any details.

“We’ve had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people, and we’ve really enjoyed it,” Trump said at the tea ceremony in the White House’s Red Room “And I think we’ve made tremendous strides. We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries.”

He also thanked the media for the “fair coverage” of the Chinese leader’s visit amid a battle with the press in which Trump had sought to block access for three organizations over their coverage of him.

Trump said he thinks U.S. farmers “are going to be very happy” because of the visit, but didn’t provide details for why.

“A lot of very positive things happened, but America is very happy about this visit, and I’m sure China is very happy also,” he said. “Great things for both countries, and it’s been just very, very productive.”

Xi for his part invited Trump and first lady Melania Trump to visit China. Trump traveled to Beijing in May to meet with Xi, but the first lady did not attend.

The Chinese leader said that during the May visit, he and Trump “agreed on the vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.”

“This time, we’ve agreed to add new substance to it, that the relationship will be a constructive one of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” he said.

He also noted that he and Trump will see each twice more this year – during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in November and the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.

data.title: US ambassador to China: 'Best thing' from Xi visit 'is to continue the conversation'
data.description:
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, defended President Trump on Friday as the U.S. leader concludes a lavish state visit with Chinese President Xi Jinping without major agreements. 

“The old adage of deliverables in a relationship that we have with China is really not measurable in many ways,” Perdue said on Fox News Channel’s “America’s Newsroom.”

“In some ways, the best thing that we accomplished in this visit is to continue the conversation,” the former Georgia Senator added.

Several Republican lawmakers expressed outward displeasure with Trump’s decision to roll out the red carpet and greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews during the Chinese president’s arrival on Wednesday. 

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) called on the president in a Wednesday floor speech to “keep in mind” during his discussions with Xi that the Chinese leader is “a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”

When pressed by Fox News’s Bill Hemmer on Friday about whether there were “any breakthroughs” at this summit, the ambassador said the leaders established an “AI dialogue” and a “crisis mechanism” for this developing technology.

“I believe that that’s going to be a platform that we can move forward on,” Perdue said. 

“This is a very bumpy road we have with China,” he added. “We’re both trying to reach strategic stability, but that doesn’t mean status quo in trade or some of these other political areas. AI is one area that we’re trying to find a way to cooperate.”

Trump has largely brushed aside rising concerns about the potential dangers posed by developing advanced AI technology. 

In a Truth Social post on Friday morning, the president called his discussion with Xi a “very productive meeting.”

“Tremendous things will be happening,” Trump wrote. “Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE. That would be “SUPER!” Everyone last night agreed, also.”

Additionally, Perdue praised Trump for pressing Xi to suspend China’s support for Iran amid the U.S.’s ongoing military operations against the country. 

“President Trump did a great job making sure China knows this is unacceptable,” Perdue said. “We’ve seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn’t the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi.”
